content: An endometrial polyp, also known as a uterine polyp, is a growth or lesion that develops in the lining of the uterus, called the endometrium. These polyps occupy space within the uterine cavity and are relatively common, affecting up to 10% of women. They can either have a broad, flat base (sessile) or be attached to the uterine wall by a thin, elongated stalk (pedunculated). Pedunculated polyps are more frequently observed than sessile ones. Their size can vary from a few millimeters to several centimeters. In cases where the polyp is pedunculated, it may extend through the cervix into the vagina. Larger polyps may contain small blood vessels. The exact cause of endometrial polyps is not well understood, but they are believed to be influenced by hormonal levels, particularly circulating estrogen, which promotes their growth. Many polyps are asymptomatic, but when symptoms occur, they may include irregular menstrual bleeding, bleeding between menstrual periods, excessively heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia), or vaginal bleeding after menopause. Bleeding from the blood vessels within the polyp can contribute to increased blood loss during menstruation or spotting between periods or after menopause. If a polyp protrudes through the cervix into the vagina, it may cause pain, a condition known as dysmenorrhea. Endometrial polyps can be diagnosed using vaginal ultrasound, sonohysterography, hysteroscopy, or dilation and curettage. However, detection via ultrasound can be challenging, especially in the presence of endometrial hyperplasia, which is an excessive thickening of the endometrium. Larger polyps may also be missed during curettage. Treatment for endometrial polyps typically involves surgical removal through curettage or hysteroscopy. During curettage, there is a risk of missing polyps, which can be minimized by first exploring the uterus with grasping forceps at the start of the procedure. Hysteroscopy allows direct visualization of the polyp, which can then be removed through the cervix. For larger polyps, they may need to be sectioned into smaller pieces before removal. If cancerous cells are identified within the polyp, a hysterectomy may be performed. However, a hysterectomy is generally not considered if cancer has been ruled out. Regardless of the method used, polyp removal is usually performed under general anesthesia. Endometrial polyps are typically benign, but some may be precancerous or cancerous. Approximately 5% of endometrial polyps contain adenocarcinoma cells. Polyps can increase the risk of miscarriage in women undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) treatment. If polyps develop near the fallopian tubes, they may contribute to difficulties in achieving pregnancy. While treatments like hysteroscopy are often effective in resolving the issue, recurrence of endometrial polyps is common. In some cases, small polyps may regress spontaneously without treatment. Endometrial polyps are most commonly found in women in their 40s and 50s. Risk factors for developing these polyps include obesity, high blood pressure, and a history of cervical polyps. The use of medications such as tamoxifen or hormone replacement therapy can also increase the likelihood of developing uterine polyps. However, the use of an intrauterine system (IUS) containing levonorgestrel in women taking tamoxifen may reduce the incidence of polyps. Endometrial polyps are present in up to 10% of women and are estimated to occur in 25% of women with abnormal vaginal bleeding. Structurally, endometrial polyps can occur as solitary growths or in clusters. They are typically round or oval in shape and range in size from a few millimeters to several centimeters in diameter. Their color is usually similar to the surrounding endometrium, appearing red or brown, although larger polyps may appear darker red. These polyps are composed of dense fibrous tissue (stroma), blood vessels, and gland-like spaces lined with endometrial epithelium. Pedunculated polyps are attached to the uterine wall by a thin stalk, while sessile polyps are connected by a flat base. Pedunculated polyps are more commonly observed than sessile ones.
